title: RSS Chief Bhagwat Addresses Thousands at Madison Square Garden Amid Protests and Sanctions Calls
excerpt: Mohan Bhagwat delivered a keynote on "universal oneness" to 6,000 attendees from 39 states and 29 countries as demonstrators rallied outside and U.S. religious freedom commissioners urged sanctions against the RSS.
body:
• RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed roughly 6,000 attendees at Madison Square Garden on August 29 as part of the organization's centenary-year international tour
  • The "Universal Oneness Celebration" drew over 250 organizations and featured a resolution by 180 religious leaders from 30 countries, while protesters assembled outside the arena
  • NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city's first Indian-American and Muslim mayor, publicly opposed the event but said the city lacked jurisdiction to cancel it
  • The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom has recommended targeted sanctions against RSS leaders, including asset freezes and entry bans

Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed thousands of Indian Americans at New York's Madison Square Garden on August 29, delivering a keynote speech at an event titled "Universal Oneness Celebration" that drew both fervent support and organized opposition.

The gathering, organized by the nonprofit American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD Forum), brought together roughly 6,000 delegates from 39 states, 850 U.S. cities, and 29 countries, according to event organizers. It marked the first stop on Bhagwat's three-nation tour of the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom to mark the RSS's centenary year.

A Message of Unity in Diversity

In his address, Bhagwat focused on themes of pluralism and fraternity, drawing parallels between American and Indian values.

https://x.com/ashoswai/status/2094332143677649222

"When we say America, the United States of America, one word is often discussed frequently: pluralism. And when we say Bharat, another word, another phrase, is discussed: unity in diversity. For Bharat, this unity and this diversity, both are in its DNA."

— Mohan Bhagwat, RSS Sarsanghchalak

Bhagwat reiterated a statement he first made in 2018: "If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu." He pointed to the RSS's 130,000 service projects across India, which he said operate without discrimination, and cited the organization's rescue efforts following a recent mid-air plane collision over Dadri, Haryana.

He distinguished between what he described as two human tendencies — those who protect only those who obey them, and those who embrace fraternity regardless of differences. "In spite of different bodies and everything being different, there is something within that is the same. We belong to each other," he said.

Before Bhagwat's address, 180 religious leaders from 30 countries announced a five-point "One World One Humanity" resolution committing to stand for the dignity of any community threatened with humiliation or violence. The leaders rejected the use of religion to justify hatred, dehumanization, or violence.

Protests and Political Opposition

Outside Madison Square Garden, demonstrators gathered to protest Bhagwat's appearance. India Today reported that protesters included separatist and pro-Palestine groups who assembled to oppose the RSS and its ideology.

More than 60 interfaith and civil-rights organizations had publicly urged the venue to cancel the event in the weeks leading up to it. A coalition organized by Hindus for Human Rights held a press conference at City Hall days before the gathering.

"If we don't stand up to religious supremacy and exclusively hateful ideologies, we will not be fulfilling our responsibility as citizens of conscience, citizens of the countries that we live in and citizens of the world."

— Sunita Viswanath, Executive Director, Hindus for Human Rights

NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city's first Indian-American and Muslim mayor, publicly opposed the event. "The vision of India that I was taught by my family and the one that I grew up being very familiar with was of a pluralistic society, of a secular republic," Mamdani said at a press conference. "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." He acknowledged, however, that the city likely lacked jurisdiction to cancel a private event.

Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander, New York City Councilmembers Shahana Hanif and Lincoln Restler, and leaders from the Indian American Muslim Council, the Interfaith Center of New York, and Riverside Church also spoke out against the gathering.

Federal Scrutiny and Sanctions Push

The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) added further pressure, with Vice Chair Asif Mahmood and Commissioner Gene Mills both condemning Bhagwat's visit. USCIRF's 2026 annual report recommended targeted sanctions against RSS leaders, including asset freezes and entry bans, and designated India a "Country of Particular Concern" for the seventh consecutive year.

The report cited RSS members as responsible for and tolerant of religious freedom violations, documenting violent acts by Hindu nationalist mobs against Christians and Muslims, including a June attack on 20 Christian families in the state of Odisha.

Supporters Rally Behind the Event

Event organizers pushed back against the criticism. Sudesh Agrawal, director of the AHEAD Forum, described the gathering as an opportunity for mutual dialogue. "Our job is to sit for a dialogue — mutual dialogue — to understand each other for the betterment of global humanity," he said.

Priya Samant, spokesperson for the event, said Bhagwat shared the stage with faith leaders from Islam, Christianity, Judaism, and Sikhism. "Oneness does not mean sameness. It means that we can work through our differences, and yet, be one big family," she told Religion News Service.

The Hindu American Foundation and HinduACTion had issued safety advisories ahead of the event, urging attendees to remain alert and report any threats to law enforcement.

What's Next

The RSS was founded in 1925 and has been banned three times in India, the first after an RSS affiliate assassinated Mahatma Gandhi in 1948. The organization is widely considered the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.

Bhagwat's international tour continues with scheduled events in Canada and the United Kingdom, where similar debates over the RSS's role and legacy are expected to follow.
